title: Opto-Electrical Detection of Donor Bound Excitons in Silicon-on-Insulator Substrate
authors: A. Kanniainen, A. S. Kumar, A. Sammak, G. Scappucci, J. T. Muhonen
abstract: Spin of a donor bound electron in silicon has been shown to be a very coherent qubit system but lacks a coherent optical interface. There does, however, exist a donor bound exciton transition that can be excited optically but decays dominantly via an Auger recombination producing an electrical signal. This provides an opto-electrical pathway for spin readout. Scaling this readout to single-spin level will require interfacing the spins with silicon photonics for efficient guiding of photons, which in turn will require moving to silicon-on-insulator (SOI) substrates. Here we demonstrate first ensemble opto-electronic measurements of donor bound excitons in SOI material, including isotopically purified 28-Si device layers. The experiments show pronounced shifts in the resonance wavelengths and broadenings of the transition linewidths compared to the bulk experiments.
summary: This paper reports on the opto-electrical detection of donor bound excitons in silicon-on-insulator (SOI) substrates, establishing a pathway for spin readout. By measuring spectral shifts and linewidths in samples of varying thickness, the authors confirm that the spin-sensitive transition survives integration into nanoscale devices. This work is vital for advancing solid-state quantum computing platforms.
main_problem: The goal is to establish a scalable opto-electrical pathway for reading out the spin state of donor electron spins in silicon, moving from bulk samples to integrated Silicon-on-Insulator (SOI) platforms.
main_result: The donor bound exciton (D^0X) transition is successfully detected in SOI substrates, showing measurable spectral shifts and broadening compared to bulk, confirming the viability of the electrical readout mechanism in integrated devices.
method: The experiment uses tunable diode lasers to excite D^0X transitions in samples of varying thickness on SOI, measuring the resulting laser-induced photoconductivity change at cryogenic temperatures.
model_or_system: The system involves donor bound excitons in silicon, whose spin state is highly coherent. The analysis utilizes the Pikus-Bir Hamiltonian to model strain effects on the valence band and the Zeeman Hamiltonian for spin splitting.
key_observables: Exciton resonance wavelength, transition linewidth ($\Gamma$), and the energy shifts caused by strain components ($\epsilon_{ij}$).
important_parameters: Device layer thickness (e.g., $1 \mu	ext{m}$ vs. $300 	ext{ nm}$), magnetic field strength (up to $400 	ext{ mT}$), and strain tensor components.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that the observed spectral shifts are dominated by strain effects, and that Fabry-Pérot interference can be accurately removed via Fourier domain filtering.
figures_summary: Figures compare exciton spectra across different silicon samples (FZ, CZ, SOI A, B, C), illustrating the spectral shifts and broadening observed in the SOI structures relative to bulk measurements.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first demonstrating the feasibility of the measurement on different SOI samples (A, B, C), then quantitatively analyzing the spectral shifts and linewidths to attribute them to strain, and finally detailing the Hamiltonian framework used to model the strain-dependent energy levels.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses the physical realization of solid-state qubits by demonstrating a robust, optically addressable, and electrically readable spin system in a scalable platform (SOI), which is crucial for quantum computing architectures.
